But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, and stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district.
But they shook off the dust of their feet against them and came to Iconium;
and the disciples were being filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; the Return to Antioch
chapters.intro: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium; many believe, but others move to stone them, and they flee to Lystra. There Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowds take the two for gods and try to sacrifice to them until they are stopped. Later Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city. The two go on to Derbe, then retrace their route, appointing elders in each church, and at last return to Antioch, where they had set out, and report.

verses.en: Now it happened in Iconium that they went together into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.
But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up and poisoned the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers.
So they stayed a considerable time, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who was bearing witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done through their hands.
But the multitude of the city was divided, and some were with the Jews and some with the apostles.

cmp.note: 这卷书只在这一章（第 4、14 节）把保罗和巴拿巴称为「使徒」；别处这个词都指耶稣选定的那十二个人。它的本义是「被派出去的人」。
cmp.en: Only in this chapter (verses 4 and 14) does the book call Paul and Barnabas "apostles"; elsewhere the word means the twelve chosen by Jesus. Its basic sense is "one who is sent out."

verses.en: And when an attempt was made by both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,
they became aware of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region,
and there they were proclaiming the good news.
And in Lystra a certain man was sitting who had no strength in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.
This man was listening to Paul speaking; and Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and was walking.
And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voice, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have become like men and have come down to us.”
And they were calling Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was before the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, crying out

and saying, “Men, why are you doing these things? We too are human beings, of like nature with you, bringing you the good news that you should turn from these empty things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.
In the generations gone by he allowed all the nations to go their own ways;
and yet he did not leave himself without witness, doing good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”
And saying these things, they scarcely restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having won over the crowds and stoned Paul, they were dragging him out of the city, supposing him to be dead.
But when the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went into the city. And on the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe.
And when they had proclaimed the good news to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying, “Through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God.”
And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, having prayed with fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
And passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia,
and having spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
and from there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been handed over to the grace of God for the work that they had completed.
And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they were reporting all that God had done with them and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they stayed no little time with the disciples.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Council at Jerusalem: Must Gentiles Be Circumcised?
chapters.intro: Men from Judea come to Antioch saying that Gentiles cannot be saved unless they are circumcised. Paul and Barnabas dispute with them, and the church sends a delegation to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem. There Peter and then James speak, and it is decided not to lay the burden of the law on the Gentiles but to write asking them to keep four things. The letter is delivered in Antioch and received with joy. Afterward Paul and Barnabas quarrel over whether to take Mark along, and go separate ways.

verses.en: And certain men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”
And when Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas and some others of them to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.

So, being sent on their way by the church, they were passing through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and they were bringing great joy to all the brothers.
And when they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.
But some of those from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
And the apostles and the elders were gathered together to look into this matter.

And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Men, brothers, you know that from early days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the good news and believe.

cmp.note: 彼得说的是第 10 章的事：他被带到外族人哥尼流家里讲道，那一家人都信了，圣灵也降在他们身上。
cmp.en: Peter is referring to chapter 10: he was brought to the house of the Gentile Cornelius to speak, the whole household believed, and the Holy Spirit came upon them.

verses.en: And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us;
and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith.
Now therefore, why are you testing God by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?
But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they also are.”
And the whole multitude fell silent, and they were listening to Barnabas and Paul describing what signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
And after they had finished speaking, James answered, saying, “Men, brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has described how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.

cmp.note: 原文这里用的是「西门」这个名字的希伯来式写法 Symeōn，书里只有这一处这样称呼彼得；和合本仍写「西门」。
cmp.en: The Greek here uses Symeōn, the Hebrew-style form of the name Simon; this is the only place in the book where Peter is so called. The Union Version writes 西门 (Xīmén, "Simon") as usual.

verses.en: And with this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written,
‘After these things I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; and its ruins I will rebuild, and I will set it up again,

cmp.note: 第 16 到 18 节引自《阿摩司书》9:11–12，照的是希腊文旧约的字句，和希伯来文本有出入。
cmp.en: Verses 16 to 18 quote Amos 9:11–12 in the wording of the Greek Old Testament, which differs from the Hebrew text.

verses.en: so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who does these things
known from of old.’
Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those from the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols and from sexual immorality and from what is strangled and from blood.

cmp.note: 「勒死的牲畜」指没有放血就宰了吃的肉。犹太律法不许吃血（旧约《利未记》第 17 章）。
cmp.en: "What is strangled" means meat from animals killed without draining the blood. Jewish law forbids eating blood (Leviticus 17).

verses.en: For Moses from ancient generations has in every city those who proclaim him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas who was called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers,
writing by their hand: ‘The apostles and the elders, brothers, to the brothers from among the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings.
Since we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, though we gave them no instructions,
it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have given up their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will also report the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these necessary things:
that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.’
So they, being sent off, went down to Antioch, and having gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter.
And when they had read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.
And Judas and Silas, being themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.
And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.
(This verse is not in the Greek edition this site follows.)

cmp.note: 较晚的抄本这里有一句话，说西拉决定仍旧留在那里。最早的抄本没有；一般认为是后来的人加进来的，为的是解释第 40 节西拉怎么还在安提阿。
cmp.en: Later manuscripts have a sentence here saying that Silas decided to remain there. The earliest manuscripts lack it; it is generally thought to have been added to explain how Silas can still be in Antioch in verse 40.

verses.en: But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming, with many others also, the word of the Lord.
And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return now and visit the brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.”
Now Barnabas wanted to take along John also, who was called Mark;
but Paul thought it best not to take along this one, who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other, and Barnabas took Mark along and sailed away to Cyprus;
but Paul chose Silas and went out, having been handed over by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
And he was going through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Timothy Joins; Over to Macedonia; the Prison at Philippi
chapters.intro: At Lystra Paul takes Timothy along. Twice the Spirit blocks their way; then in a vision at night Paul sees a Macedonian asking for help, and they cross the sea to Philippi. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, believes and has them stay with her. Paul drives a spirit of divination out of a slave girl; her owners bring him before the magistrates, and he and Silas are beaten and jailed. At midnight an earthquake comes, and the jailer and his household believe. From verse 10 the narrative begins to say "we."

verses.en: And he came also to Derbe and to Lystra. And look, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but of a Greek father,
who was well spoken of by the brothers in Lystra and Iconium.
Paul wanted this man to go out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
And as they were going through the cities, they were delivering to them, to keep, the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem.
So the churches were being strengthened in the faith and were increasing in number daily.
And they went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia;
and when they came opposite Mysia, they were trying to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them;
and passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a certain Macedonian man was standing and begging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
And when he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to proclaim the good news to them.

cmp.note: 原文从这一节起，叙述里第一次用「我们」，此前一直是「他们」。这样的段落书里有四处：16:10–17、20:5–15、21:1–18、27:1–28:16。
cmp.en: From this verse the narrative says "we" for the first time; until now it has been "they." There are four such stretches in the book: 16:10–17; 20:5–15; 21:1–18; 27:1–28:16.

verses.en: So, putting out to sea from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the following day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of that district of Macedonia, a colony. And we were staying in this city for some days.

cmp.w: prōtē tēs meridos Makedonias polis, kolōnia
cmp.note: 前半句各抄本写法不一，意思也有两种理解：「马其顿那一区的头等城市」或「马其顿第一区的一座城」。kolōnia 是从拉丁文借来的词，指罗马安置退伍军人、享有罗马法律地位的城；和合本译「驻防城」。
cmp.en: The manuscripts vary in the first phrase, and it can be taken two ways: "a leading city of that district of Macedonia" or "a city of the first district of Macedonia." Kolōnia is a loanword from Latin for a city settled with Roman veterans and holding Roman legal status; the Union Version has 驻防城 (zhùfáng chéng, "garrison city").

verses.en: And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and sitting down we were speaking to the women who had come together.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple goods from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, was listening; and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to the things spoken by Paul.
And when she was baptized, and her household, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us.
And it happened, as we were going to the place of prayer, that a certain slave girl who had a spirit of divination met us, who was bringing her masters much profit by fortune-telling.

cmp.note: 字面是「一个皮同的灵」。皮同是希腊神话里守着德尔斐神谕处的大蛇，这个词后来指能替人占卜的灵；和合本译「巫鬼」。
cmp.en: Literally "a python spirit." The Python was the serpent that guarded the oracle at Delphi in Greek myth, and the word came to mean a spirit that tells fortunes; the Union Version has 巫鬼 (wūguǐ, "sorcery demon").

verses.en: She followed after Paul and us and was crying out, saying, “These men are slaves of the Most High God, who proclaim to you a way of salvation.”
And she was doing this for many days. But Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
But when her masters saw that their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers,
and bringing them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are throwing our city into confusion, being Jews,
and they are proclaiming customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or to practice, being Romans.”
And the crowd rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off them and were ordering them to be beaten with rods.
And when they had laid many blows on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to guard them securely;
who, having received such a charge, threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them;
and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken, and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds came loose.
And the jailer, being roused from sleep and seeing the doors of the prison opened, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out with a loud voice, saying, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
And calling for lights, he rushed in, and trembling, he fell down before Paul and Silas,
and bringing them outside, he said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
And they said, “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.
And taking them at that hour of the night, he washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all who were his.
And bringing them up into his house, he set food before them, and he rejoiced greatly with his whole household, having believed in God.
And when day came, the magistrates sent the officers, saying, “Release those men.”
And the jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word that you be released. Now therefore come out and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “Having beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Romans, they threw us into prison; and now are they throwing us out secretly? No indeed; rather let them come themselves and bring us out.”

cmp.note: 字面是「罗马人」，这里指有罗马公民身份的人；按罗马的法律，公民没有经过审判不可以鞭打。和合本照字面写「罗马人」。
cmp.en: Literally "Romans," here meaning men who hold Roman citizenship; under Roman law a citizen could not be flogged without trial. The Union Version keeps the literal 罗马人 (Luómǎ rén, "Romans").

verses.en: And the officers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,
and coming, they appealed to them, and bringing them out, they were asking them to leave the city.
And going out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house, and when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Thessalonica, Berea, and Paul’s Speech in Athens
chapters.intro: Paul and Silas reach Thessalonica, where Paul argues in the synagogue that Jesus is the Christ; some believe, and some of the Jews stir up a riot. Sent off by night to Berea, they find hearers who check the scriptures every day, until the troublemakers follow them there. Paul is escorted to Athens, is disturbed by a city full of idols, and is brought by philosophers to the Areopagus. Verses 22 to 31 are his speech there.

verses.en: Now having passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
And according to Paul’s custom he went in to them, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the scriptures,
opening them and setting forth that the Christ had to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This is the Christ, the Jesus whom I proclaim to you.”
And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great multitude of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women.

But the Jews, becoming jealous and taking along some wicked men from among the market idlers and forming a mob, set the city in an uproar; and attacking the house of Jason, they were seeking to bring them out to the people.
And not finding them, they were dragging Jason and some brothers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also,
and Jason has received them; and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”
And they stirred up the crowd and the city officials who heard these things,
and having taken security from Jason and the rest, they released them.
And the brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea; and when they arrived they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
Now these were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Many of them therefore believed, and not a few of the Greek women of standing and of the men.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul in Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds.
And then immediately the brothers sent Paul off to go as far as the sea, and both Silas and Timothy remained there.
And those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and having received a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.
Now while Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he was reasoning in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

And some also of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers were conversing with him. And some were saying, “What would this seed-picker wish to say?” And others, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign divinities,” because he was announcing the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.

cmp.note: 字面是「捡种子的」，本来说的是啄食谷粒的鸟，引申为东听一句、西捡一句就到处卖弄的人。和合本译「胡言乱语的」。
cmp.en: Literally "seed-picker," first said of birds pecking up grain and then of a person who picks up scraps of learning here and there and shows them off. The Union Version has 胡言乱语的 (húyán luànyǔ de, "one who talks nonsense").

verses.en: And taking hold of him they brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that is being spoken by you?
For you are bringing some strange things to our ears; we wish therefore to know what these things mean.”
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there spent their time in nothing other than telling or hearing something newer.
And Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.

cmp.note: 这个词可以是好话（很敬神），也可以是坏话（很迷信），听的人怎么理解都行。和合本译「很敬畏鬼神」。
cmp.en: The word can be a compliment ("very devout") or a criticism ("very superstitious"), and a hearer could take it either way. The Union Version has 很敬畏鬼神 (hěn jìngwèi guǐshén, "much in awe of spirits and gods").

verses.en: For as I passed through and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed, ‘To an unknown god.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands,
nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things.
And he made from one every nation of men to dwell on all the face of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwelling,
that they should seek God, if perhaps they might grope for him and find him, though indeed he is not far from each one of us.
For ‘in him we live and move and are,’ as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’

cmp.note: 保罗这里引的是希腊诗人的话。后一句「我们也是他的子孙」一般认为出自公元前三世纪的诗人亚拉图（他写的是宙斯）；前一句有人认为也是引诗，出处说法不一。
cmp.en: Paul is quoting Greek poets. The second line, "For we are also his offspring," is generally traced to the third-century BCE poet Aratus, who wrote it of Zeus; the first line is taken by some to be a quotation too, though its source is disputed.

verses.en: Being therefore the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man.
So then, having overlooked the times of ignorance, God now commands all people everywhere to repent,
because he has fixed a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.”
Now when they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some were mocking, but others said, “We will hear you about this yet again.”
So Paul went out from their midst.
But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · Paul in Corinth; Apollos in Ephesus
chapters.intro: Paul comes to Corinth, works as a tentmaker with the couple Aquila and Priscilla, and preaches in the synagogue; when the Jews oppose him he turns to the Gentiles and stays a year and a half. The Jews bring him before the proconsul Gallio, who refuses to hear the case. Paul then returns by way of Ephesus to Antioch and sets out again to visit the disciples. The chapter closes with Apollos arriving in Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila explain the way to him more accurately.

verses.en: After these things he left Athens and came to Corinth.
And finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, he went to them,
and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
And he was reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath and trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
Now when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was wholly occupied with the word, solemnly testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
But when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”

cmp.w: To haima hymōn epi tēn kephalēn hymōn
cmp.note: 字面是「你们的血在你们头上」，是旧约里就有的说法，意思是后果由你们自己负责。和合本把「血」译成「罪」。
cmp.en: Literally "your blood on your head," a phrase already found in the Old Testament, meaning that the consequences are your own responsibility. The Union Version turns "blood" into 罪 (zuì, "guilt").

verses.en: And moving on from there he went into the house of a certain man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
And Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his household; and many of the Corinthians, hearing, were believing and being baptized.
And the Lord said to Paul in the night through a vision, “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were some wrongdoing or wicked crime, O Jews, I would with reason have borne with you;
but since it is questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves; I am not willing to be a judge of these things.”
And he drove them from the judgment seat.
And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and were beating him in front of the judgment seat; and none of these things concerned Gallio.
Now Paul, having stayed many days longer, took leave of the brothers and was sailing away for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; at Cenchreae he had his hair cut, for he had a vow.
And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
And when they asked him to stay a longer time, he did not consent,
but taking leave of them and saying, “I will return to you again, God willing,” he set sail from Ephesus.
And landing at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and went down to Antioch.
And having spent some time there he departed, passing successively through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus; he was mighty in the scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he was speaking and teaching accurately the things about Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue; but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
And when he wished to cross over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him; and when he arrived he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,
for he was vigorously refuting the Jews in public, showing by the scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · Paul in Ephesus; the Silversmiths’ Riot
chapters.intro: Paul reaches Ephesus, meets some disciples who have received only John’s baptism, and baptizes them in the name of Jesus. He teaches there for over two years, and God does many mighty works through him; some men who use the name of Jesus to drive out spirits are beaten instead, and many burn their books of magic. Then the silversmith Demetrius, whose trade in the goddess Artemis is suffering, stirs the whole city into a riot, which the town clerk finally talks down.

verses.en: And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found some disciples,
and he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said to him, “No, we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.”
And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” And they said, “Into John’s baptism.”
And Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”
And when they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they were speaking in tongues and prophesying.
And they were in all about twelve men.
And entering the synagogue, he was speaking boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some were becoming hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
And this went on for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
And God was doing extraordinary mighty works through the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his skin to the sick, and the diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.
But some also of the itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to name over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
And seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered and said to them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I am acquainted with, but who are you?”
And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

cmp.note: 这个词本义是「两个」，当时的口语里也可以指「全部」。前面说的是七个儿子，所以白话和英文取「全都」；和合本取本义，译「其中二人」。
cmp.en: The word properly means "both," but in the everyday Greek of the time it could also mean "all." Seven sons have just been mentioned, so both translations here take it as "all"; the Union Version keeps the strict sense with 其中二人 (qízhōng èr rén, "two of them").

verses.en: And this became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived in Ephesus; and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was being magnified.
And many of those who had believed were coming, confessing and declaring their practices.

And a considerable number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and were burning them before all; and they counted up the value of them and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So mightily the word of the Lord was growing and prevailing.
Now when these things were completed, Paul resolved in the spirit, having passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”

cmp.note: 字面是「在灵里」。可以指保罗自己的心（和合本「心里定意」，白话也这样译），也可以指圣灵的带领；原文两种读法都可以。
cmp.en: Literally "in the spirit." It can mean Paul’s own mind, as the Union Version and the Chinese here take it (心里, xīnlǐ, "in his heart"), or the leading of the Holy Spirit; the Greek allows either.

verses.en: And having sent into Macedonia two of those who ministered to him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a time.
Now about that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, was bringing no little business to the craftsmen.
Gathering these together, with the workmen of similar trades, he said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our prosperity,
and you see and hear that not only at Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that gods made with hands are not gods.

And not only is there danger that this trade of ours will come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she will even be brought down from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.”
And when they heard this they were filled with rage and were crying out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
And the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, Paul’s traveling companions.
And when Paul wished to go in among the people, the disciples would not let him;
and some also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
So then some were crying out one thing and some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and the majority did not know why they had come together.
And some of the crowd instructed Alexander, the Jews having put him forward; and Alexander, motioning with his hand, wished to make a defense to the people.

cmp.note: 这个词在这里是什么意思不很确定：可以是「向他说明情况」「指点他」，也可以是「把他推举出来」。和合本取后一种，译「把亚力山大从众人中带出来」。
cmp.en: What this verb means here is not certain: "informed" or "instructed him," or else "brought him forward." The Union Version takes the second sense: 把亚力山大从众人中带出来 (bǎ Yàlìshāndà cóng zhòngrén zhōng dài chūlái, "brought Alexander out of the crowd").

verses.en: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, one voice arose from all of them, crying out for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he says, “Men of Ephesus, who is there among men who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from heaven?

cmp.note: 字面是「从宙斯那里落下来的」，也就是「从天上落下来的」，指一件被当作女神像来拜的东西。和合本译「从丢斯那里落下来的像」，「丢斯」就是宙斯。
cmp.en: Literally "fallen from Zeus," that is, "fallen from the sky," said of an object venerated as the goddess’s image. The Union Version has 从丢斯那里落下来的像 (cóng Diūsī nàlǐ luò xiàlái de xiàng, "the image that fell from Zeus"), where 丢斯 is Zeus.

verses.en: Since then these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and to do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are in session and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another.
But if you seek anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.

For indeed we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today, there being no cause, concerning which we will not be able to give an account of this gathering.” And having said these things he dismissed the assembly.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 · A Night at Troas; Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
chapters.intro: Paul leaves Ephesus, travels through Macedonia to Greece and back again, and meets his companions at Troas. During a night gathering a young man falls from the third story and Paul restores him. The party then sails south. At Miletus Paul sends for the elders of the church in Ephesus and takes leave of them; verses 18 to 35 are his words. From verse 5 on the narrator says "we," counting himself among the travelers.

verses.en: And after the uproar had ceased, Paul, having sent for the disciples and encouraged them, took his leave and departed to go into Macedonia.
And having gone through those parts and encouraged them with many words, he came into Greece
and spent three months there; and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
And there accompanied him Sopater of Berea, the son of Pyrrhus; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
And these, having gone ahead, were waiting for us at Troas;
and we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas within five days, where we stayed seven days.
And on the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul was conversing with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight.
Now there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.

And a certain young man named Eutychus, sitting on the windowsill, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul conversed still longer; overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead.
But Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”
And having gone up and broken the bread and eaten, and having talked with them a long while until daybreak, so he departed.
And they brought the boy away alive, and were comforted not a little.
But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for so he had arranged, intending himself to go on foot.
And when he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene,
and sailing from there, on the following day we arrived opposite Chios, and the next day we put in at Samos, and the day after we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if it were possible for him, on the day of Pentecost.
And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called for the elders of the church.
And when they had come to him, he said to them, “You know how I was with you the whole time, from the first day that I set foot in Asia,
serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews;
how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house,
solemnly testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now, behold, bound in the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will befall me there,

cmp.note: 字面是「在灵里被捆绑」。可以指被圣灵催逼着非去不可（白话这样译，下一节接着说的正是圣灵），也可以指保罗自己心里放不下；和合本取后一种，译「心甚迫切」。
cmp.en: Literally "bound in the spirit." It may mean that the Holy Spirit compels him to go, as the Chinese here takes it (the next verse goes on to speak of the Holy Spirit), or that Paul himself feels inwardly constrained; the Union Version takes the latter: 心甚迫切 (xīn shèn pòqiè, "my heart is very pressed").

verses.en: except that the Holy Spirit solemnly testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions await me.

But I do not count my life of any value as precious to myself, so that I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify solemnly to the good news of the grace of God.
And now, behold, I know that all of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face no more.
Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean from the blood of all,

cmp.w: katharos eimi apo tou haimatos pantōn
cmp.note: 字面是「对所有人的血，我是干净的」，和 18:6 是同一种说法，意思是：该讲的我都讲了，谁灭亡都不是我的责任。和合本把意思直接译了出来。
cmp.en: Literally "I am clean from the blood of all," the same idiom as in 18:6: I have said all I had to say, and no one’s ruin is my responsibility. The Union Version translates the sense directly: 你们中间无论何人死亡、罪不在我身上 (nǐmen zhōngjiān wúlùn hé rén sǐwáng, zuì bù zài wǒ shēnshang, "whoever among you perishes, the guilt is not on me").

verses.en: for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.
Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood.

cmp.note: 这半句有两种读法：「用他自己的血」，或者「用他自己那一位（指他儿子）的血」。另外，有些抄本作「主的教会」而不是「上帝的教会」。白话和英文照字面取第一种，没有解释。
cmp.en: This phrase can be read two ways: "through his own blood," or "through the blood of his Own," meaning his Son. Some manuscripts also read "the church of the Lord" instead of "the church of God." Both translations here keep the first, literal reading without explaining it.

verses.en: I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;
and from among your own selves men will arise speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them.
Therefore keep awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease to admonish each one with tears.
And now I commit you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me.
In all things I showed you that by laboring in this way we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

cmp.w: Makarion estin mallon didonai ē lambanein
cmp.note: 耶稣的这句话，四卷福音书里都没有记载，只见于这里。
cmp.en: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels; it is found only here.

verses.en: And having said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
And there was much weeping by all, and falling on Paul’s neck they were kissing him,
grieving most of all over the word that he had spoken, that they were going to see his face no more. And they were accompanying him to the ship.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 · Up to Jerusalem; Arrested in the Temple
chapters.intro: Paul and his companions sail to Tyre and then to Caesarea; all along the way people urge him not to go to Jerusalem, and the prophet Agabus foretells that he will be bound, but he will not be persuaded. In Jerusalem, James and the elders ask him to join four men in a rite of purification so that people will see he keeps the law. As the seven days are ending, he is seized in the temple by a crowd that has been stirred up, and the Roman commander takes him away. The "we" of the first eighteen verses is the narrator himself.

verses.en: And when it came about that we set sail, having torn ourselves away from them, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara;
and finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
And having come in sight of Cyprus and leaving it on the left, we were sailing to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
And having found the disciples, we stayed there seven days; and they were telling Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem.

And when it came about that our days there were completed, we departed and were going on our way, all of them with wives and children accompanying us until we were out of the city; and kneeling down on the beach and praying,
we said farewell to one another, and we went on board the ship, and they returned home.
And having completed the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and having greeted the brothers we stayed with them one day.
And on the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him.
Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
And as we were staying there many days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea,

and coming to us and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘In this way the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is, and will hand him over into the hands of the Gentiles.’”
And when we heard these things, both we and the local people were urging him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
And since he would not be persuaded, we fell silent, saying, “The will of the Lord be done.”
And after these days we made ready and were going up to Jerusalem.
And some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing us to a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
And when we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
And on the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.
And having greeted them, he was relating one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.

And when they heard it they were glorifying God, and they said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law;
and they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles apostasy from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children nor to walk according to the customs.
What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Therefore do this that we tell you: we have four men who have a vow upon themselves;

take these and purify yourself along with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; and all will know that there is nothing in the things they have been told about you, but that you yourself also walk in line, keeping the law.

But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we wrote, having decided that they should keep themselves from what is sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality.”

cmp.note: 这里说的信和决定，就是第 15 章耶路撒冷会议之后写给外族信徒的那封信（15:23–29）。
cmp.en: The letter and the decision mentioned here are those of chapter 15, written to the Gentile believers after the meeting in Jerusalem (15:23–29).

verses.en: Then Paul took the men, and on the next day, having purified himself along with them, he went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for each one of them.
Now when the seven days were about to be completed, the Jews from Asia, having seen him in the temple, were stirring up all the crowd and laid hands on him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place; and besides, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple.
And the whole city was stirred, and the people ran together; and taking hold of Paul they were dragging him out of the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
And as they were seeking to kill him, a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
And he at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them; and when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up and took hold of him and ordered him to be bound with two chains, and he was inquiring who he was and what he had done.
But some in the crowd were shouting one thing and some another; and since he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.
And when he came to the steps, it came about that he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the multitude of the people was following, crying out, “Away with him!”
And as he was about to be brought into the barracks, Paul says to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek?
Are you not then the Egyptian who some days ago stirred up a revolt and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?”

cmp.note: 字面是「带匕首的人」，是从拉丁文借来的词，指当时一批用短刀暗杀对手的犹太激进分子。和合本译「凶徒」。
cmp.en: Literally "dagger men," a word borrowed from Latin for a group of Jewish militants of the time who assassinated opponents with short knives. The Union Version has 凶徒 (xiōngtú, "ruffians").

verses.en: But Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city; and I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.”
And when he had given permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people; and when there was a great silence, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying,

cmp.note: 字面是「希伯来话」。一般认为这里指的是当地犹太人平常说的亚兰话，它和希伯来话很接近。
cmp.en: Literally "the Hebrew language." It is generally thought to mean here Aramaic, the closely related language that local Jews ordinarily spoke.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 · Paul’s Defense on the Steps; a Roman Citizen
chapters.intro: Standing on the barracks steps, Paul tells the crowd his own story: a Jew strictly trained in the law, he had persecuted those who believed in Jesus; on the road to Damascus a great light struck him down and he heard Jesus speak to him; later, in the temple, he was told to go to the Gentiles. At that word the crowd shouts for his death. The commander orders him examined by scourging, and Paul discloses that he is a Roman citizen. Verses 3 to 21 are Paul’s words.

verses.en: “Men, brothers and fathers, hear my defense that I now make to you.”
And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he says,

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated according to the strictness of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women,

as also the high priest and the whole council of elders bear me witness; from whom I also received letters to the brothers and was journeying to Damascus to bring those also who were there bound to Jerusalem to be punished.
And it happened that as I was journeying and drawing near to Damascus, about midday, suddenly a great light from heaven flashed around me,
and I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’
Now those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me.

cmp.note: 原文是「没有听见声音」。第 9 章第 7 节讲同一件事，说同行的人「听见声音，却看不见人」。和合本这里译「没有听明」，把两处接了起来；白话和英文照这一节的原文译。
cmp.en: The Greek says they "did not hear the voice." Acts 9:7, telling the same event, says his companions were "hearing the voice but seeing no one." The Union Version here writes 没有听明 (méiyǒu tīng míng, "did not hear clearly"), joining the two accounts; both translations here follow this verse as it stands.

verses.en: And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about all that has been appointed for you to do.’
And since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I came into Damascus led by the hand of those who were with me.
And a certain Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,
came to me, and standing by said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And in that very hour I looked up at him.
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will and to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth,
for you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard.
And now why do you delay? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’
And it happened that when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’
And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I was imprisoning and beating those who believed in you;
and when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself also was standing by and approving and guarding the garments of those who were killing him.’
And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”
And they were listening to him up to this word, and then they raised their voices, saying, “Away with such a fellow from the earth, for he ought not to live!”
And as they were shouting and throwing off their garments and flinging dust into the air,
the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by scourging, so that he might find out for what reason they were shouting against him so.
But when they had stretched him out with the thongs, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman and uncondemned?”
And when the centurion heard it, he went to the tribune and reported, saying, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman.”
And the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” And he said, “Yes.”
And the tribune answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum.” And Paul said, “But I was even born one.”
Immediately therefore those who were about to examine him withdrew from him; and the tribune also was afraid when he learned that he was a Roman and that he had bound him.

But on the next day, wishing to know for certain why he was being accused by the Jews, he released him and ordered the chief priests and all the Sanhedrin to assemble, and having brought Paul down, he set him before them.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 · Before the Council; the Plot; Sent to Caesarea by Night
chapters.intro: Paul stands before the council and says he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection; Pharisees and Sadducees fall to quarreling, and the tribune takes him back to the barracks. That night the Lord tells him he must testify in Rome too. More than forty Jews swear to kill him; his nephew reports it, and the tribune sends him under guard by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea.

verses.en: And Paul, looking intently at the council, said, “Men, brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.”
And the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit judging me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law order me to be struck?”
And those standing by said, “Do you revile the high priest of God?”
And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he is high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

cmp.note: 引自旧约《出埃及记》22:28。
cmp.en: Quoted from Exodus 22:28.

verses.en: Now Paul, knowing that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, cried out in the council, “Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead I am being judged.”
And when he said this, a dispute arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but Pharisees acknowledge them all.

And there was a great outcry, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, saying, “We find nothing wrong in this man; and what if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel—”

cmp.w: ei de pneuma elalēsen autōi ē angelos
cmp.note: 原文这句话没有说完。较晚的抄本在后面加了一句「我们不要与上帝作对」；和合本补的是「怎么样呢」。
cmp.en: In the Greek the sentence breaks off unfinished. Later manuscripts add “let us not fight against God”; the Union Version supplies 怎么样呢 (zěnmeyàng ne, “what then?”).

verses.en: And as the dispute grew violent, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down and seize him from among them and bring him into the barracks.
And the following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.”
And when it was day, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves by a curse, saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
And there were more than forty who made this plot.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said, “We have bound ourselves by a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
Now therefore, you with the council give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine his case more exactly; and we are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
But the son of Paul’s sister heard of the ambush, and he came and entered the barracks and told Paul.
And Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.”
So he took him and brought him to the tribune and says, “The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.”
And the tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked privately, “What is it that you have to report to me?”
And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more exactly about him.

But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him; and now they are ready, waiting for the promise from you.”
So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.”
And he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, and seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, from the third hour of the night;

cmp.note: 这个词意思不确定，字面像是「右手拿着（武器）的」，通常译成长矛手或轻装兵。和合本译「长枪手」。
cmp.en: The meaning of this word is uncertain; literally something like “those who hold (a weapon) in the right hand,” usually rendered spearmen or light-armed troops. The Union Version has 长枪手 (chángqiāngshǒu, “spearmen”).

verses.en: and provide mounts for Paul to ride, and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”
And he wrote a letter to this effect:
‘Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
And wishing to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found him accused over questions of their law, but having no charge deserving death or chains.
And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.’
So the soldiers, according to their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
And on the next day they let the horsemen go on with him and returned to the barracks.
When these came into Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also to him.
And having read it, he asked from what province he was, and learning that he was from Cilicia,
he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers also arrive,” and he ordered him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 · The Hearing before Felix
chapters.intro: Five days later the high priest Ananias comes to Caesarea with an advocate, Tertullus, and accuses Paul before the governor Felix of stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point, admitting only that he worships God according to “the Way” and hopes for the resurrection of the dead. Felix puts the case off until the tribune arrives, keeps Paul for two years, and leaves him in custody when his term ends.

verses.en: And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate, one Tertullus, and they laid their case against Paul before the governor.
And when he was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since reforms are being made for this nation by your foresight,
in every way and everywhere we accept this, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
But so as not to detain you further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.
For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we seized him.
(This verse is not in the Greek edition this site follows.)

cmp.note: 较晚的抄本从第 6 节末到第 8 节开头多出一段话，意思是：我们本要按我们的律法审他，千夫长吕西亚却来了，用强力把他从我们手里夺走，又吩咐告他的人到你这里来。最早的几份抄本没有这一段，一般认为是后来加进来的，所以底本不收。和合本把这几句都印成小字注。
cmp.en: From the end of verse 6 to the start of verse 8, later manuscripts have an extra passage meaning: we wanted to judge him by our own law, but the tribune Lysias came and with great force took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you. The earliest manuscripts lack it, and it is generally thought to be a later addition, so the edition leaves it out. The Union Version prints these sentences as small-print notes.

verses.en: By examining him yourself you will be able to learn about all these things of which we accuse him.”
And the Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.
And when the governor nodded to him to speak, Paul answered, “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense.
As you can verify, it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,
and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.

But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything that is in accordance with the Law and that is written in the Prophets,

cmp.note: 和第 5 节「拿撒勒人那一派」是同一个词，本义是「派别」。和合本在这里译「异端」，在第 5 节译「教党」。
cmp.en: The same word as in verse 5 (“the sect of the Nazarenes”); its basic sense is “party” or “school.” The Union Version translates it here as 异端 (yìduān, “heresy”) and in verse 5 as 教党 (jiàodǎng, “religious faction”).

verses.en: having a hope in God, which these men themselves also await, that there is going to be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.
In this I myself also strive always to have a blameless conscience toward God and toward people.
Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings.
While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, with no crowd and no uproar.
But there were some Jews from Asia—they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, if they have anything against me.
Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council,
unless it is about this one utterance that I cried out as I stood among them: ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today.’”
But Felix, knowing rather accurately the things about the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.”
And he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody and have some liberty, and that none of his own people be prevented from attending to him.
And after some days Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jew, and he sent for Paul and heard him about faith in Christ Jesus.
And as he discussed justice and self-control and the judgment to come, Felix became afraid and answered, “Go away for the present, and when I find time I will summon you.”
At the same time he was also hoping that money would be given him by Paul; so he sent for him rather often and conversed with him.
But when two years had passed, Felix received a successor, Porcius Festus; and wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in chains.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 · Paul Appeals to Caesar
chapters.intro: The new governor Festus takes office, and the Jewish leaders ask him to send Paul back to Jerusalem, meaning to kill him on the road. Festus holds court at Caesarea and asks Paul whether he will be tried in Jerusalem; Paul appeals to Caesar. Some days later King Agrippa visits, Festus lays the case before him, and the next day Paul is brought in.

verses.en: Now Festus, having arrived in the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
And the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews laid their case against Paul before him, and they were urging him,
asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem, while they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.
Festus then answered that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to go there shortly.
“So,” he says, “let those among you who have authority come down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them accuse him.”
And after staying among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought.
And when he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges that they could not prove,
while Paul said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews nor against the temple nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.”
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and there be judged before me on these matters?”
But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you also know very well.
If then I am in the wrong and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die; but if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar.”

cmp.note: 罗马公民受审时，有权要求把案子交给皇帝审理；说了这句话，地方长官就不能再自己判了。
cmp.en: A Roman citizen on trial had the right to ask that his case be heard by the emperor; once this was said, the local governor could no longer decide it himself.

verses.en: Then Festus, having conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”
Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to greet Festus.
And as they were staying there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid their case, asking for a sentence against him.
To them I answered that it is not the custom of the Romans to hand over anyone before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make a defense concerning the charge.
So when they had come together here, I made no delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought.
When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge of such evils as I was supposing,
but they had certain questions against him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died, whom Paul asserted to be alive.
And being at a loss how to investigate these matters, I asked whether he wished to go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of the Emperor, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him up to Caesar.”

cmp.note: 原文是「可敬者」，罗马皇帝的尊号（拉丁文 Augustus 的希腊文说法）。和合本译「皇上」。
cmp.en: Literally “the Revered One,” the honorific of the Roman emperor (the Greek for Latin Augustus). The Union Version has 皇上 (huángshàng, “His Majesty the Emperor”).

verses.en: And Agrippa said to Festus, “I myself also would like to hear the man.” “Tomorrow,” he says, “you shall hear him.”

So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp and had entered the audience hall with the tribunes and the prominent men of the city, at the command of Festus Paul was brought in.

And Festus says, “King Agrippa and all you men present with us, you see this man about whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and since he himself appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him.

About him I have nothing definite to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after the examination has taken place, I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate also the charges against him.”

chapters.title: Chapter 26 · Paul’s Defense before King Agrippa
chapters.intro: King Agrippa lets Paul speak for himself. Paul tells his life: raised a strict Pharisee, he persecuted those who believed in Jesus; on the road to Damascus a light struck him down, and he heard Jesus speaking to him and sending him to the Gentiles. Festus says he is out of his mind; Agrippa says he could have been released. Verses 2 to 23 are all Paul speaking.

verses.en: And Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense:
“I consider myself fortunate, King Agrippa, that it is before you I am to make my defense today concerning all the things of which I am accused by Jews,
especially because you are familiar with all the customs and questions among Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.
My manner of life from my youth, which from the beginning was spent among my own nation and in Jerusalem, all Jews know.
They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee.
And now I stand here being judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
to which our twelve tribes hope to attain as they earnestly worship night and day. For this hope I am accused by Jews, O king.
Why is it judged incredible among you that God raises the dead?
I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene.
And this I did in Jerusalem: I both locked up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them.

cmp.note: 字面是「投下了石子」：古时用小石子表决。和合本译「出名定案」。
cmp.en: Literally “I cast down a pebble”: votes were once cast with small stones. The Union Version has 出名定案 (chūmíng dìng’àn, “put my name to the verdict”).

verses.en: And in all the synagogues, punishing them often, I tried to force them to blaspheme, and being furiously enraged at them, I pursued them even to foreign cities.
In this connection I was traveling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,
when at midday along the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

cmp.note: 当时的一句俗语：牛去踢赶牛人手里的尖棍，只会伤着自己。
cmp.en: A proverb of the time: an ox that kicks at the driver’s pointed stick only hurts itself.

cmp.note: 「希伯来话」在这里一般认为指当地犹太人平常说的亚兰话。
cmp.en: “The Hebrew language” here is generally taken to mean Aramaic, the everyday speech of the Jews of that region.

verses.en: And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

But rise and stand on your feet; for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you a servant and witness both of the things in which you have seen me and of those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you

to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’
Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of repentance.
For these reasons Jews seized me in the temple and were trying to kill me.
So, having obtained help from God, to this day I stand testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said was going to happen:
that the Christ would suffer, and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”
And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus says with a loud voice, “You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you out of your mind.”
But Paul says, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am uttering words of truth and sound sense.
For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak freely; for I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian!”

cmp.w: en oligōi me peitheis Christianon poiēsai
cmp.note: 「en oligōi」可以是「用很短的时间」，也可以是「用几句话」；这句话是认真还是讥讽，原文看不出来。白话取「几句话」，英文取「很短的时间」。
cmp.en: The phrase en oligōi can mean “in a short time” or “with few words,” and the Greek does not show whether the remark is earnest or ironic. The Chinese takes “with a few words”; the English takes “in a short time.”

verses.en: And Paul said, “I would pray to God that, whether in a short time or a long time, not only you but also all who hear me today might become such as I am, except for these chains.”
And the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those sitting with them,
and when they had withdrawn, they were speaking to one another, saying, “This man is doing nothing deserving death or chains.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

chapters.title: Chapter 27 · The Voyage to Rome; Storm and Shipwreck
chapters.intro: Paul and other prisoners sail for Italy in the charge of a centurion named Julius. At Crete Paul urges them to go no farther, but no one listens. Soon after they put to sea a gale catches the ship, and it drifts for fourteen days. Paul says an angel of God has told him that everyone aboard will live. In the end the ship runs aground in a bay, and all two hundred seventy-six reach land. The “we” of this chapter is the narrator, who is on board too.

verses.en: And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.

cmp.note: 字面是「可敬者的营」，一支以皇帝尊号命名的部队。和合本译「御营」。
cmp.en: Literally “the cohort of the Revered One,” a unit named after the emperor’s honorific. The Union Version has 御营 (yùyíng, “the imperial battalion”).

verses.en: And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the places along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
And the next day we put in at Sidon; and Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for.
And putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.
And when we had sailed across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.
And there the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board.
And sailing slowly for many days and arriving with difficulty off Cnidus, as the wind did not allow us to go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
Now since much time had passed and the voyage was already dangerous, because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul advised them,

cmp.note: 指犹太人的赎罪日，在秋天（九、十月间）。过了这个时候，地中海上风浪大，古时一般就不再远航了。
cmp.en: The Jewish Day of Atonement, in autumn (September or October). After that season the Mediterranean grew stormy, and in antiquity long voyages generally stopped.

verses.en: saying to them, “Men, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion was persuaded more by the pilot and the owner of the ship than by what Paul said.

And because the harbor was not suitable for wintering in, the majority reached a decision to put to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest, and winter there.

cmp.note: 字面是「朝着西南风和西北风」。和合本译「一面朝东北，一面朝东南」，是把这句话理解成顺着这两种风吹去的方向看。
cmp.en: Literally “looking toward the southwest wind and the northwest wind.” The Union Version has 一面朝东北，一面朝东南 (“facing northeast on one side and southeast on the other”), taking the phrase to mean the direction toward which those winds blow.

verses.en: Now when a south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close inshore.
But not long after, a tempestuous wind, called Euraquilo, struck down from the land.

cmp.note: 水手给东北风起的名字。
cmp.en: The sailors’ name for the northeast wind.

verses.en: And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
And running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat.
After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship; and fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and so were driven along.

cmp.note: 「放下器具」具体指什么不确定：可能是收帆，也可能是放下拖在水里减速的锚具。和合本译「落下篷来」。
cmp.en: What exactly “lowering the gear” means is uncertain: it may be taking in sail, or letting down a sea anchor to drag and slow the ship. The Union Version has 落下篷来 (luòxià péng lái, “let down the sail”).

verses.en: And as we were violently storm-tossed, the next day they began to jettison the cargo,
and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.
And when neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned.
